summary: Two wooden range towers on Noir Point, Cape Breton, lined up through the Great Bras d'Or shoals from 1903. Electrified 1956, automated by 1993, closed to visitors.

structures.type: square wooden tower, white pyramid with red upper portion

access.note: Both towers closed to visitors. The front tower stands on private property behind a house at the end of a lane; the rear grounds are described as open in one directory and closed in another.

events.note: Sites selected at Duffus Point for range lights to guide between the shoals at the entrance
Range buildings erected; put in operation on the opening of navigation in 1903. Front tower on Noir Point, rear tower 1,689 ft from it.
Electrified 7 November 1956; colour changed from fixed white to fixed green
March 1958: sun switches and battery backup lights fitted; range de-staffed
Front tower lowered by one foot (1968 to 1970)
Vertical red stripes added to both towers
NSLPS lists the front light as automated by 1993

resolved_conflicts.explanation: The 1901 report names Duffus Point and the 1902 report puts the work at Duffus point on the northern side of Boularderie Island; the 1903 report, which describes the working towers, puts the front tower on Noir Point on the west side of Boularderie Island. The reports do not explain the change, and LighthouseFriends uses both names. The record's Noir Point location is kept.
The 1902 report names Peter McFarlane as contractor and the 1903 report names P. L. McFarlane of Baddeck. Both are McFarlanes; the reports do not say whether they are one man.

The Rowlett directory says the rear site is open and its tower closed; LighthouseFriends says the rear grounds are closed. The story states the disagreement, says both sources show the tower closed, and does not choose.

notes_for_editor: Canadian station: no USLHS roster, so keepers come from the Marine reports (fiscal 1900 to 1924 corpus) and LighthouseFriends (LF). LF is copyrighted: facts only, paraphrased in the story. Keeper check: the 1904 keepers' table (Marine report, 1905 Sessional Paper) lines up McLean, Malcolm with Great Bras d'Or Range, Front Light by position in its columns (names, stations and dates read from the same column order). The rear light's keeper line (Fraser) could not be matched in the Marine tables we read; he rests on LF alone. The 1903 report gives the front tower 31 ft high and the light 41 ft above high water (12.5 m); the Coast Guard list gives a focal height of 15.7 m and the tower 9.9 m. The sources do not explain the difference. The 1903 report says visible 11 and 13 miles without saying nautical. The Coast Guard list marks the front light seasonal; NSLPS dates automation to 1993 but LF says de-staffed 1958 and caretakers to about 1969, so the automation date is uncertain. The rear grounds are open per Rowlett and closed per LF; I treated them as closed. NSLPS 'Site Access: By Car' for the front light is wrong for a private-property tower and was not used. Chronicling America search for the range (1900-1930): no station-linked pages. Suggested record change: add first_lit 1903 (the record has null). Fact-check 2026-10-28: the McLean row on the 1904 keepers' table (scan p.175, printed p.162) is still matched by column position and was not checked against the page image: the built-in browser refused archive.org, so the image could not be viewed. The rear light's grounds are reported open by Rowlett and closed by LighthouseFriends; the story now states the disagreement instead of choosing one.
